questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Present perfect and the simple past
questions.learningObjective: choose the simple past when the time frame named is closed
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Ayer terminé el informe y se lo envié a la directora.' Why can a preterite carry a word like ayer at all, when the present perfect is the ordinary tense for the past?

options.text: Ayer fixes a period that is shut, so the actions read as finished and located
Ayer is a vague word, so the preterite steps in to fill a gap in the present perfect
options.misconception: treats a precise day as if the choice of tense depended on vagueness of time

options.text: A preterite is required whenever a verb other than tener appears somewhere in the sentence
options.misconception: believes the tense is chosen by the verb rather than by the time frame

options.text: The present perfect refuses any word naming a day, so a speaker has to convert the tense
options.misconception: believes the present perfect cannot take a word for a closed period

questions.explanation: The two tenses both reach into the past, and the choice turns on one question: is the stretch of time the sentence points at still open or already shut. Ayer, la semana pasada, en 2020 and esa mañana once the morning is over all name closed periods, and for those Spanish uses the preterite, which presents the action as complete and pinned down. The present perfect is kept for open frames such as hoy, este mes or en lo que va del año, where the period is still running and the result may still bear on the present. The rule a learner can check is simply whether the named period can still receive another action; if it cannot, the preterite is the form the language wants.
questions.hint: Ask whether another action could still be added to the day that is named.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Present perfect and the simple past
questions.learningObjective: use the present perfect inside a period that is still running
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Esta semana he leído dos informes y todavía no he escrito el tercero.' What is the present perfect doing in that sentence?

options.text: It holds both actions inside a period that is still running, so the third is still outstanding
It marks the two reports as finished and the third as something that cannot be begun
options.misconception: reads an outstanding task as one the speaker has given up on entirely

options.text: It pushes the reading far into the past and leaves the writing as a plan for later
options.misconception: assumes the present perfect sets the actions at a remote distance instead

options.text: It separates the two acts in time so that reading must finish before writing starts
options.misconception: reads a shared time frame as a requirement about the order of two tasks

questions.explanation: Esta semana is an open frame: the week named has not ended, so a third report could still be added to it, and a present perfect keeps both acts inside that same running period. The presence of a third item that has not happened is the clearest signal that the period is open, because a closed frame would have made the set complete. The rule is the same one that governs ayer: a period that can still receive an action takes the present perfect, and a period that cannot take the preterite. The reading is therefore not merely earlier than the writing in a timeline, it shares a single unfinished container with it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the week named could still receive a third report.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: read a present perfect result beside an imperfect background
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'He cerrado la ventana porque hacía frío.' Which verb reports the state that still held when the window was shut, and why?

options.text: The imperfect, since a state with no stated end is what it reports, and the shutting happened inside that state
The preterite, since shutting a window is one completed act with a clear beginning and an end
options.misconception: confuses which of the two clauses describes and which one narrates an act

options.text: The present perfect, since both halves of the sentence are placed inside the same morning
options.misconception: believes a shared time word forces the same tense in both clauses

options.text: The conditional, since a reason given for an action is always a hypothetical rather than a fact
options.misconception: assumes a stated cause in the past is by definition counterfactual

questions.explanation: Hacía frío describes a state that was running and had no stated end, which is exactly what the imperfect reports, and the window was shut inside that state rather than at any particular point in it. The present perfect belongs to the other half, since the shutting has a result the speaker is living inside now, namely that the cold outside has stopped. A learner who puts the preterite on hacía implies the cold began and ended at a known moment, which the sentence refuses to say, and a learner who makes both halves perfect drags an open-ended state into a closed tense.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two states had a beginning and an end the speaker can name.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: keep a continuing arrangement in the present with desde and a start point
questions.stem: A family has rented the same flat without a break since 2019 and intends to stay on. Which sentence says exactly that, and only that?

options.text: La familia alquila la casa desde 2019 y no piensa mudarse
La familia alquiló la casa desde 2019 y no piensa mudarse
options.misconception: puts a preterite on an arrangement the facts say is still running

options.text: La familia alquilaba la casa desde 2019 y no pensaba mudarse
options.misconception: uses the imperfect for a state that has not been closed yet

options.text: La familia alquiló la casa en 2019 y desde entonces no se ha mudado
options.misconception: tells the same story as an event completed once rather than a state still open

questions.explanation: Alquilar with desde and a starting point that is still running takes the present tense, because the arrangement has not been closed and the family is still inside it. The preterite with desde would open the tenancy at 2019 and shut it again, leaving a gap before the present that the facts do not allow, and the imperfect would place the tenancy inside a period now over rather than inside the present. Option D is close in sense but it uses a preterite for the opening and a present perfect for the continuity, which describes an event completed once rather than a state that is still running. The rule to check is whether the arrangement is current.
questions.hint: Ask whether the tenancy is still running at the moment of speaking.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: mark one completed span of time against a habit inside it
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Durante cinco años vivió en Valparaíso y cada verano volvía a Buenos Aires.' What does the change of tense mark in that pair?

options.text: The first verb sets one completed stretch of time; the second shows a habit repeated inside that stretch
The first verb is an error, because a stretch of years can only be reported with the imperfect
options.misconception: holds that a stated length of time is too bounded for the preterite

options.text: The two verbs carry the same meaning and the change between them is a matter of taste alone
options.misconception: believes a contrast of tenses can be decorative rather than structural

options.text: The second verb reports a single return, while the first says he never left the country at all
options.misconception: reads an imperfect as a single event and reverses what the first clause says

questions.explanation: Vivió with a stated length of time opens and closes a block of years, and the preterite is the tense for a block treated as finished, while volvía reports something that happened again and again with no particular occurrence singled out. The two are not alternatives; the second is set inside the first, and the pair is how Spanish says he lived in one city for a fixed period and repeatedly came back during it. A learner who reverses the pair loses the shape of the period, and one who uses the imperfect for the five years would be suggesting the period has no end.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the sentence is bounded and which part repeats.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: read the imperfect as a state of a period rather than a dated act
questions.stem: An old porter says, 'De joven llevaba un uniforme con galones.' What does the imperfect contribute to that sentence?

options.text: It presents the uniform as the state his life had in that period, not as one dated act
It reports one morning when he put the uniform on for the first and only time
options.misconception: reads a description of a period as a single first occasion

options.text: It says the uniform is being worn by him again now as he stands at the door
options.misconception: ignores the time phrase that confines the statement to his youth

options.text: It marks the sentence as something the speaker now doubts that is true
options.misconception: treats the imperfect as a marker of doubt about a statement

questions.explanation: The imperfect describes a state or a picture as it stood across a stretch of life, so de joven llevaba carries the sense of a condition of that period rather than of an event placed at a point. A preterite would turn the uniform into something he donned on one occasion, which is not what a career-long habit of dress is, and a present perfect would tie the uniform to the present, which the phrase de joven excludes. The check a learner can apply is whether the verb is describing how things were or recording that something happened, and this verb is describing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sentence describes a way of being or a single thing done.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: read the imperfect as a wish or state that was never realised
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Cuando era niño, quería ser bombero.' What is the imperfect doing, given that the wish never came true?

options.text: It sets the wish inside the period of childhood, so it reads as an intention of that time
It says the wish was formed once and then abandoned on the same afternoon
options.misconception: reads a preference of a period as a single decision taken in an afternoon

options.text: It claims the wish is still held now and can still be acted on if the chance arises
options.misconception: ignores the phrase that places the wanting in the speaker's childhood

options.text: It reports a wish the speaker has now forgotten ever having formed at all
options.misconception: treats the imperfect as a signal of forgetting rather than of description

questions.explanation: Querer in the imperfect describes a disposition that belonged to a period and was never carried out, so the sentence says that during his childhood he wanted to be a fireman, not that he wanted it once on a particular day. The unfulfilled wish is precisely why the imperfect is at home here: the condition of wanting outlasted many moments and none of them brought the thing itself. A preterite would report one act of wanting on one occasion, which understates a childhood-long preference, and the present tense would claim the wish is live now, which the opening phrase rules out.
questions.hint: Ask how long the wanting lasted, and whether it ever arrived.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Conditional sentences of the first type
questions.learningObjective: identify the real condition and its consequence
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Si el tren llega puntual, llegamos a la reunión a las nueve.' What is each verb contributing to that sentence?

options.text: The if-clause states a condition and the main clause states what follows, with both in the present
The if-clause states a hope and the main clause states a doubt about whether it will happen
options.misconception: reads an ordinary expectation as a mixture of hope and doubt

options.text: The if-clause reports an event of last week and the main clause predicts from that event
options.misconception: puts a past frame on a sentence that names no past time at all

options.text: The if-clause sets a condition against the facts and the main clause hedges what is believed
options.misconception: turns a realistic condition into an unreal one that the speaker doubts

questions.explanation: This is the plainest of the three conditional shapes, a condition the speaker regards as realistic together with the result that follows if it holds, and Spanish builds it with si followed by the present and a main clause in the present or the simple future. Llega and llegamos are both present because nothing in the sentence places either one in the past or sets the condition unreal. A learner who reaches for the conditional here has turned an ordinary expectation into a daydream, and a learner who puts the future in the if-clause adds a time the sentence never mentioned.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker thinks this outcome is a realistic one.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Conditional sentences of the second type
questions.learningObjective: identify the unreal condition of a second-type conditional
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Si tuviera más tiempo, aprendería a tocar el chelo.' What does the imperfect subjunctive mark in that opening clause?

options.text: The condition is set against the facts, so the clause describes a situation treated as unreal
The condition is likely to be met, so the clause states an expectation about the coming weeks
options.misconception: reads a hypothetical condition as a confident forecast about the future

options.text: The condition refers to a period that has closed, so the clause reports what was once true
options.misconception: treats the sentence as a report about a period that has already ended

options.text: The condition is a concession, so the clause argues against what the main clause claims
options.misconception: reads an if-clause as a concession rather than as a condition

questions.explanation: The second type sets a condition that the speaker does not believe to hold, and Spanish marks that unreality by putting the past imperfect in the subjunctive after si, so tuviera is the shape the verb takes whenever the condition is hypothetical rather than open. The main clause then carries the simple conditional, here aprendería, so the whole sentence looks one step away from the facts and can never be called a mistake. A learner who writes tengo in the if-clause claims to have the time, which is exactly what the sentence denies, and a learner who writes tenía would merely report an old state without the unreal quality.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker has the free time or is only pretending to.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Conditional sentences of the third type
questions.learningObjective: identify the unreal past condition and its past result
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Si hubiera estudiado medicina, sería médico en un hospital pequeño.' What does each part of that sentence do?

options.text: The if-clause sets an unreal condition in the past and the main clause gives its result back then
The if-clause states a known fact about the past and the main clause predicts a later result
options.misconception: reads a hypothetical past condition as something that actually happened

options.text: The if-clause states a certainty about his studies and the main clause expresses regret for a promise
options.misconception: turns a counterfactual condition into a real certainty plus a complaint

options.text: The if-clause reports what another person has said and the main clause repeats their claim as fact
options.misconception: treats the sentence as reported speech rather than as a conditional structure

questions.explanation: The third type looks back at a condition that cannot be met now, so the if-clause takes the pluperfect subjunctive hubiera estudiado and the main clause takes the conditional imperfect sería, which is the conditional of the past. The whole sentence is a single look backwards, and that is why neither part can be put in a present tense. A learner who writes estudió would be reporting a fact, and a learner who writes será in the main clause would be projecting the outcome into the future, when the outcome the sentence is about would have been reached long ago.
questions.hint: Ask whether the condition could still be met today or not.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: form the imperfect subjunctive of an -ar verb after a wish
questions.stem: A learner must fill the blank in 'Ojalá el jefe ___ en la reunión de mañana.' Which form does the language want here, and why that spelling?

options.text: Hablara, because a verb ending in -r keeps the -ra ending the imperfect subjunctive requires
Hablará, because a wish in Spanish is expressed with the simple future and nothing else
options.misconception: believes a wish is a prediction about the future rather than a preference

options.text: Hablasen, because ojalá is one of the triggers that takes the present subjunctive
options.misconception: groups ojalá with cuando and para que as a trigger of the present subjunctive

options.text: Hablar, because after a wish the bare infinitive is enough and the ending is optional
options.misconception: believes an infinitive can stand alone as the verb of a complete wish clause

questions.explanation: The imperfect subjunctive of an -ar or -er verb is built on the stem of the present subjunctive with -ra, -se or a raise in writing, and that third person singular form is what the language reaches for here. Hablará looks close because it is the simple future, but a wish after ojalá is not a prediction, so the future does not fit. The present subjunctive hablasen belongs with triggers such as cuando, mientras or para que, and a bare infinitive would leave the wish without a person to have it, which Spanish never allows in this frame.
questions.hint: Ask which family of endings the third person singular of the imperfect subjunctive belongs to.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: read an emotion trigger as making its complement a supposition
questions.stem: A colleague says, 'Me alegra que el proyecto empiece en enero.' What does the subjunctive on empiece tell the reader?

options.text: That the start is treated as uncertain, so the feeling is about a possibility not a fact
That the start happened already, so the feeling is being reported as a finished event
options.misconception: reads the trigger as reporting a fact the speaker is sure of

options.text: That the project is certain to begin, which is the reason the verb agrees in the negative
options.misconception: links the mood to negation although the sentence has no negative in it

options.text: That the speaker doubts the project exists, since doubt is what the subjunctive marks here
options.misconception: assumes every subjunctive signals doubt rather than emotion or supposition

questions.explanation: Expressions of feeling such as me alegra, me molesta, me sorprende and me da pena take the subjunctive when the thing felt is not a completed fact, and the imperfect is used because the start lies ahead or outside the speaker's knowledge. The trigger here is positive, and that matters: the mood has nothing to do with negation, since the sentence contains none. A learner who links the subjunctive to a negative will leave this correct sentence alone and still change a wrong one after me molesta, so what has to be recognised is the trigger and not the punctuation.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: tell an assumed likeness from an asserted one after como si
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Este hombre habla como si supiera el tema.' Why is the verb in the subjunctive in that clause?

options.text: Como si with the subjunctive presents the likeness as the speaker supposes it, not as a fact
Como si always takes the subjunctive, whatever the speaker believes to be the case in life
options.misconception: treats como si as a fixed trigger instead of a choice of mood

options.text: The subjunctive is there because saber can never appear in a clause with the indicative
options.misconception: blames the identity of the verb rather than the meaning of the comparison

options.text: Habla is the subjunctive, and the second verb only has to follow the mood of the first
options.misconception: calls the indicative verb subjunctive and looks in the wrong clause

A learner who treats como si as a fixed trigger will miss that the same word carries both, and a learner who thinks the second verb copies the mood of the first is looking in the wrong clause, because the verb that carries the comparison is the one inside the si-clause.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker is sure the resemblance is real or only suggesting it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: order the conditional types by how nearly their conditions are treated as fact
questions.stem: Three conditional sentences are set out below, each with an if-clause and a main clause. Which sequence runs from the condition nearest to being a fact to the one furthest from it?

options.text: Si tengo fiebre, me quedo en casa, an ordinary expectation about tomorrow
Si tuviera fiebre, me quedaría en casa, a condition the speaker does not expect to meet
Si hubiera tenido fiebre, me habría quedado en casa, a condition that cannot be met at all

questions.explanation: The three types are not a list of interchangeable shapes but a scale of distance from what the speaker believes. The first type uses the present in both parts because the condition is a realistic expectation, the second moves the if-clause into the imperfect subjunctive because the condition is posited against the facts, and the third moves it again to the pluperfect because the condition lies in a time that has closed. A learner who learns the three as unrelated patterns tends to pick the one that sounds most formal, so the scale is what makes the choice: first decide how firmly the speaker believes the condition, and the tenses follow from that.
questions.hint: Ask, for each sentence, whether the condition could still be met today.

questions.learningObjective: screen a set of sentences for the unreal conditions that need the subjunctive
questions.stem: Five conditional sentences have been written. Three of them use the if-clause to state a condition the writer does not believe to hold, so they need the imperfect subjunctive. Which three?

Si tuviera tiempo, escribiría una novela entera

questions.learningObjective: identify each trigger separately rather than assuming one rule for the text
questions.stem: A report reads: 'Es probable que la comisión se reúna en abril. Los vecinos piden que se publique el proyecto antes de esa fecha y el gerente ha dicho que no descarta aplazar la reunión.' Which of the three finite verbs carries a subjunctive, and for what reason?

Pidan, because pedir is the verb that obliges another person to act on the request

options.text: Descarte, because a clause after ha dicho reports speech and reported speech needs a subjunctive
options.misconception: supposes that any clause after a verb of saying must be subjunctive

options.text: Se reúna and pidan, because Spanish requires the subjunctive in every subordinate clause
options.misconception: believes every subordinate clause in Spanish takes the subjunctive

questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Ojalá no hubiera llovido el día de la boda.' What does the form hubiera llovido consist of, and what does the pair express?

The imperfect of haber plus a participle, describing rain that fell repeatedly through that period
options.misconception: reads the auxiliary as the imperfect and the whole phrase as a repeated habit

options.text: The simple past of haber plus a participle, reporting the rain as a fact that really occurred
options.misconception: reads a wish as a report of something the speaker knows really happened

Because the auxiliary is the past perfect, the rain is placed earlier than some other past moment rather than inside a running period. The three other shapes are real constructions with different work, since the imperfect plus participle covers a span, the preterite plus participle reports a fact, and the conditional plus participle projects a result forward from a past point.

questions.learningObjective: put a wish about the past in the pluperfect rather than the imperfect
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Ojalá me hubieran dado el libro a tiempo.' What does the choice between hubiera dado and habían dado turn on?

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: teach the choice between the imperfect and the pluperfect subjunctive as a question about position
questions.stem: Explain to a learner how Spanish decides between the imperfect subjunctive and the pluperfect subjunctive, and say what each of the two places in relation to.

answer.exemplar: The decision is a question about where the speaker is standing, not about how the event feels. A verb in the imperfect subjunctive stands inside a period the speaker can still picture as a whole: el dinero que me hacía falta, the money I used to need, and ojalá tuviera tiempo, I wish I had time, where the shortage or the spare time is a state of that period and is not over. A verb in the pluperfect subjunctive stands before a point inside that period and can no longer be moved: ojalá me hubieran llamado, I wish they had called, where the call would have changed a decision already taken. The pairing to memorise is a present wish with the imperfect and a past wish with the pluperfect, and a learner who gets it wrong usually hears the two as stronger and weaker rather than as early and late. A second test is available: the imperfect subjunctive still describes a situation that could in principle continue, while the pluperfect describes one closed by the moment of speaking, which is why a wish about a person the speaker would like to have now uses the imperfect and a wish about a meeting that is over uses the pluperfect.

questions.explanation: Two past subjunctives are only learnable as one idea, because a learner who meets them as a pair of unrelated endings will pick between them by feel and be wrong regularly. The pair is really a single scale of time, with the imperfect marking a state of a stretch and the pluperfect marking an act that lies before a point inside that stretch. Once the scale is understood, the commonest errors explain themselves: a learner who writes ojalá me llamaran for something that plainly never happened has put the regret inside a period, and a learner who writes ojalá tuviera for a childhood that has ended has put a lost period in front of a point that has closed. Both mistakes are the same mistake, which is a position in time chosen on the wrong side of the speaker.
questions.hint: Ask whether what is being wished about could still go on, or whether it is already closed.

questions.learningObjective: place an action before a point in the future with the future perfect
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Para el jueves habré terminado el manuscrito.' What is that tense doing in the sentence?

options.text: Placing the finishing before a future point, so the work counts as done as of Thursday
Placing the finishing after a future point, so Thursday is when the writing will begin
options.misconception: reads a completion before a deadline as a beginning after it

options.text: Reporting that the work was finished long ago and that the date is mentioned only now
options.misconception: reads a future auxiliary as a report about something already completed

options.text: Expressing a doubt about whether the writing will ever be brought to an end at all
options.misconception: reads the same structure as if it were the one used in a sentence of fear

questions.explanation: The future perfect is built on the future of haber plus a participle, and it locates the action before a point in the future, so habré terminado says that by Thursday the manuscript is finished and that the state of being finished already holds at that moment. The simple future would say the work will be done at some moment without saying it is done in advance, and the present perfect would tie the finishing to the present, which is not what a deadline set in advance means. The same structure carries a doubt, as in cuando llegue habré terminado, so a learner who meets the form in both places should read it as a position in front of a moment and not as a promise or a fear.
questions.hint: Ask whether the work is done before Thursday or at some point during it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: place a completion before a point in the future with the conditional perfect
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Para esas fechas ya habríamos vendido el local.' What does the form habríamos vendido express?

options.text: That the sale would be complete before that date, since the conditional perfect places it earlier
That the sale is under way now and continues until that date, since the auxiliary is a present one
options.misconception: reads the conditional auxiliary as a present tense and misses the participle

options.text: That the sale happened before a date in the past, since the conditional is used for the past
options.misconception: confuses the conditional perfect with the conditional of the past

options.text: That the sale may or may not take place, since an auxiliary in the conditional marks uncertainty
options.misconception: treats the conditional as a mood of doubt rather than as a tense

questions.explanation: The conditional perfect is the third person plural of the conditional of haber, habría, followed by a participle, and it locates the action before a point in the future in the same way the future perfect locates it in the indicative. Ya is the ordinary signal that a point in the future has been passed in the sentence's own frame, so habríamos vendido says the sale is done and that the state of having sold already holds at that date. The word ya in the answer about uncertainty has no business there, because the conditional is not a mood of doubt but the tense that carries an unreal or projected past, and the simple conditional without a participle says nothing about completion at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the participle adds to the auxiliary, and what ya is doing.

questions.learningObjective: say what the future perfect adds to a clause about the future
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Cuando llegues, ya habré salido.' What does the second clause add to what the first one already leaves open?

options.misconception: reads a relation of time in the second clause as a relation of cause

options.text: It turns a statement about the future into one about the moment of speaking as it stands now
options.misconception: reads a claim about a later point as a claim about the present

options.text: It reports that the speaker has already left some time before the other person arrives
options.misconception: reads a future perfect as a claim that the leaving is already behind us

The two clauses are joined by cuando, which marks time, and the work of the second is to say which side of that time the leaving falls on.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: put a wish about an open situation in the imperfect subjunctive
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Ojalá viviera más cerca del trabajo.' Which tense does that wish require, and what makes it the right one?

options.text: The imperfect subjunctive, because the wish concerns a state that is still open and could still change
The present indicative, because the speaker is describing a circumstance as it actually is
options.misconception: treats a wish as though it were a description of the real state of things

options.text: The simple future, because a wish in Spanish is always a prediction of what will happen
options.misconception: confuses a wish about the present with a claim about the future

options.text: The pluperfect subjunctive, because a wish is always about something that has already ended
options.misconception: sends an open situation to the wrong side of the moment of speaking

questions.explanation: A wish about a circumstance the speaker would like to be different but which is still changing is expressed with the imperfect subjunctive, and viviera is that form, because the state of living near the work is one that could still be altered before it settles. The present indicative is what makes a learner hesitate, since the circumstance is real, but a wish reports a preference about the world rather than a description of it, and it is the ojalá that supplies the unreality.
questions.hint: Ask whether the situation being wished about could still be changed tomorrow.

options.misconception: turns a command passed to someone else into the manager's own wish

options.text: Hay que with a gerund, which makes the fetching of the plans the manager's own task
options.misconception: loses the person the order was aimed at behind a general obligation

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: name what the tense of a report measures after a change of tense
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'El jefe dijo: "Mañana no voy."' Three days later she reports, 'El jefe dijo que no iba.' What has the report done to the statement?

options.text: Moved the statement further into the past, and the tense of the verb has moved with it
Left the original moment in place, so the verb should have stayed in the present as it was
options.misconception: insists the report is made at the moment of the statement itself

options.text: Turned a statement of fact into a report of what somebody thinks the case to be
options.misconception: reads reported speech as an opinion rather than as a change of tense

options.text: Changed the sense of the negative, so that a denial has become a refusal to do anything
options.misconception: believes a tense shift can change what a negative denies

questions.explanation: A report takes its verbs one step further back than the moment of speaking, so a statement made in the present about the future becomes imperfect in the report, and iba does that work. The shift is not a change of meaning but a change of vantage point: the report is not a denial of tomorrow, it is a denial as it stood three days ago. A learner who keeps the present in the report makes the whole account sound as though it were happening now, which misleads a reader about when the boss spoke, and the second reading loses the report's own position in time altogether.
questions.hint: Ask how many days separate the moment of speaking from the moment of the original statement.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: track the change of person in a reported exchange
questions.stem: A witness said, 'Yo no vi el camión; mi compañero sí lo vio.' A journalist put the testimony this way: 'El testigo dijo que él no había visto el camión y que su compañero lo había visto.' What has happened to the pronouns between the two versions?

options.text: The first person has become a third person, and the possessive has stayed with the companion it belonged to
Both first person forms have been kept, so nothing in the testimony has actually changed at all
options.misconception: expects a report to preserve the pronouns of the original speaker

options.text: The first person has been kept for the witness and dropped for the companion, reversing the report
options.misconception: attributes the sight to the wrong person in the reported clause

options.text: The pronouns have been dropped, since a reported clause in Spanish can carry no subject of its own
options.misconception: believes a Spanish reported clause cannot name its own subject

questions.explanation: A report normally turns the original first person into a third person tied to the person reporting, which is why yo becomes él here, and the change of tense has done the same work to the verb. The possessive is the delicate part: mi compañero becomes su compañero inside a clause whose subject is el testigo, so the reference stays with the witness and the sighting is still attributed to the companion rather than to the witness. A learner who rewrites the companions as su keeps the words but loses the sense, and one who keeps yo inside a clause introduced by el testigo said produces a report that contradicts itself.
questions.hint: Ask who the subject of dijo is, and whose companion su refers to in the clause that follows.

questions.learningObjective: tell an imperative turned into a report from an order softened into a request
questions.stem: A director told a secretary, 'Deje la llave en recepción.' The secretary passed it on: 'El director te ha dicho que dejes la llave en recepción.' What does the change from deje to que dejes show?

options.misconception: reads a change of mood as a change in how firmly the order is meant

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: How far a report reaches back
questions.learningObjective: order reports by how far the moment of speaking has moved past the statement
questions.stem: One speaker says, 'Vendré el lunes.' Four people report that statement, and the four reports are set out below. Which sequence orders them from the smallest gap to the largest?

options.text: A report made a minute later: dijo que vendría, since the future is still ahead of the reporter
A report made a week later: dijo que vendría, since a past report keeps the future one step on
A report made a year later: dijo que había venido, since the statement now lies well inside the past
A report made ten years later: dijo que había venido, since no present tense reaches that far back

questions.explanation: A report has one job, which is to show the statement from the position of the person reporting it, and the further back that position is, the further the verbs have to travel. A minute and a week are both recent enough that the Monday is still a future for the reporter, so the imperfect carries it in both cases; a year and ten years are not, so the statement is now a thing that happened and the pluperfect carries it. The tempting order puts the two imperfect reports together and the two pluperfect reports together, which is right about the pairs and wrong about the sequence, since what changes steadily is the distance and not the tense.
questions.hint: Ask for each report how much time separates the speaker from the statement.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: separate the changes a report requires from those it merely allows
questions.stem: A student turns a direct sentence into a report and gets 'Ella dijo: "Voy a llamarte"' back as 'Ella dijo que iba a llamarte.' Three of the changes below are required by that report rather than chosen by the writer. Which three?

options.text: The verb is put in the imperfect, since the statement is now something said and not something happening
The subject pronoun is dropped, since the person reporting is now the subject of the sentence
The conjunction que is added, so the statement can be fitted inside a clause of saying
options.misconception: believes a report can be attached to dijo with no connective at all

options.text: The final vowel of the verb is dropped, so the report can be joined to the word before it
options.misconception: treats a change of written form as part of what a report does to a verb

questions.explanation: Three of these are what a report is made of. The imperfect comes from the reporting verb, since a statement is a past act of saying and its verbs follow it back one step; the subject pronoun is dropped because the subject is now ella, the person who spoke, and Spanish lets a pronoun go when the verb already says who; and que is the hinge that turns a statement into a clause of saying, which is why ella dijo, voy is not a sentence a Spanish speaker will accept. The fourth is a question of how a word is attached when it is spoken, not of what a report does, and a report made in writing keeps the full form.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four changes is about tense, about who is doing the saying, and about structure.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: teach the tense shift of reported speech as a single change of point of view
questions.stem: Explain to a learner why a Spanish speaker reports what someone said in the imperfect rather than in the tense the original sentence used, and say what that shift is measuring.

answer.exemplar: The shift measures the distance between the moment of speaking and the moment of the statement, and it is the reporting verb that creates that distance. When someone speaks now, what they say is happening now and what they mention is still ahead of them; by the time somebody else repeats it, that now has passed, so what was coming has become something that was expected and what was expected has become something that already happened. That is why a future verb such as vendré arrives in a report as iba, and why a verb that was already in the past arrives as había venido. The rule a learner can hold is short: move every verb in the reported clause one step further into the past than it stood at the moment of speaking, and then move it once more if the report itself is now old enough for a present tense to have lost its grip. A learner who wants a check should look at the reporting verb itself, because dice and decía are present and imperfect respectively, and their tense is the tense every other verb in the report has to match.

questions.explanation: Learners who are taught the shift as a list of pairs end up memorising van a ir became iba without knowing why, and the list breaks the moment a sentence contains a verb they have not met in that pair. The single rule is more useful than the list, because it explains every pair at once and it explains what happens when there is no matching pair at all. Once the shift is understood as a change of vantage point rather than as a change of tense for its own sake, a learner can also handle a report inside a report, where the second report moves the verbs one step further back again, and can see why a journalist repeating something from ten years ago uses the pluperfect where a colleague repeating it from this morning uses the imperfect.
questions.hint: Ask what the tense of the reporting verb is doing, and what every other verb is being made to match.

questions.learningObjective: recognise a se that has no subject and is not a passive
questions.stem: A report says, 'Se necesita un conductor para el turno de noche.' What is the se in that sentence?

options.text: An impersonal se standing for the passive, since the driver is needed without anyone doing the needing
A reflexive pronoun, since a driver is preparing the van before the night shift begins
options.misconception: supplies a subject for the se and an action the sentence never mentions

options.text: A passive with a known agent, since the report says who is requiring a driver for the shift
options.misconception: invents an agent in order to turn an impersonal se into a personal passive

options.text: A form of dar with the pronoun se attached, since the report is handing over a responsibility
options.misconception: supplies a verb the sentence does not contain to explain the se

A reflexive reading would need a subject to reflect, and there is none, and a passive reading with a known agent would require the agent in the sentence, which is absent. Dar appears nowhere in the construction, so that reading supplies a verb the text does not use. The check a learner can apply is to ask who did it, and an answer of nobody is the sign of an impersonal se rather than a passive one.
questions.hint: Ask who needs the driver, and whether the sentence says so.

questions.topic: From an event to a generalisation
questions.learningObjective: order the three ways of saying a thing from the most particular to the most general
questions.stem: Four sentences report the same matter at four different levels of generality. Which sequence runs from the most particular report to the broadest generalisation?

options.text: Se cometen errores en esa empresa con más frecuencia de la debida, with the event dropped
Dos revisores encontraron tres errores en el informe de ayer, naming both the agent and the day
Se encontraron tres errores en el informe de ayer, which keeps the day and drops the agent
En cualquier empresa pueden cometerse errores, which drops the place, the count and the date

The second keeps the occasion and the count and drops the agent, which is what a reflexive passive does, and the third keeps the verb and the frequency and drops the event entirely, which is what an impersonal se does. questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: teach a learner's test for telling the three constructions apart
questions.stem: Explain to a learner how to decide whether a se in a Spanish sentence is reflexive, passive or impersonal, and say what question settles each case.

answer.exemplar: One question settles it: who is doing the thing. Se lava el coche los sábados is reflexive, because the person washing is inside the sentence and is also who the car belongs to, so the action comes back to the subject. Se repararon las farolas is a passive, because the thing repaired, the lamps, is in the sentence while the people who repaired them are not, and Spanish marks the missing half with se in front of a third person singular verb. En esa zona se avería con frecuencia la red is impersonal, because nothing at all is presented as doing anything: the sentence reports a recurring fact about a place, and if a subject were supplied it would not be the one the sentence means. A learner who asks who is doing it will find a subject in the first case, no subject in the second, and no place for a subject in the third, and that difference is the whole test. The two passive forms are worth separating as well, since se repararon and fueron reparadas by una cuadrilla are not variants: the first is the ordinary way of not naming an agent, and the second is the way of naming one with por.

questions.explanation: Learners meet three constructions built on the same four letters and are given three rules that do not connect, so they end up guessing from the shape of the verb. One test connects them, and the test is about the subject rather than about the meaning of the verb. The proof that the test works is that the same verb can occur in more than one of the three, since se lava is reflexive with el coche and passive with las camisas, and a rule about the verb alone cannot decide anything. A second test is worth adding for the passives, since a learner who treats the two passives as interchangeable will write se reparó cuando un electricista lo reparó and produce a report that says the same thing twice, and the fix is to remember that naming the agent requires the other passive.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: explain the causative as an idea rather than as a list of verb pairs
questions.stem: Explain to a learner what a causative construction does in Spanish, and show why the same idea is expressed with tener, hacer and mandar in different sentences.

answer.exemplar: A causative reports somebody causing something to happen rather than doing it, and Spanish marks the cause with a verb of possession, obligation or command followed by an infinitive or a participle. Se ha hecho instalar la puerta says somebody arranged for the door to be fitted; hay que limpiar los filtros says somebody has to see to the filters; lo mandó reparar says he sent it to be mended. The three carriers are not decoration, because each answers a different question. Tener plus participle, as in tiene arreglada la caldera, says the work is already done and the speaker is the one who got it done, which is how a Spanish speaker reports a repair without claiming to have made it. Hacer plus infinitive, as in hizo instalar la puerta, says the speaker arranged it and the arrangement is the point. Mandar plus infinitive, as in mandó revisar el contrato, adds a step: the work leaves the speaker and is done by somebody else. What they share is that a second person stands behind the action, and what separates them is whether that person has been got to do it yet.

questions.explanation: A learner who is given a table of verb pairs will produce correct sentences in a drill and then freeze in real writing, because the choice depends on a question the table does not ask. The question is where the work has got to: done, arranged, or sent out, and each of the three carriers answers it. The most common error in the classroom is tener plus participle, which sounds finished and is often used for something still wanted, and the reason it is hard is that a Spanish speaker says the boiler is mended as soon as the mender has been in, so the perfect does the work an English speaker does with a past participle. Understanding the causative as an idea rather than a list is what lets a learner produce a sentence that was never in the table.
questions.hint: Ask at what point the work has reached, and which of the three carriers matches that point.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Gerund and infinitive after a verb
questions.learningObjective: teach the choice of a gerund or an infinitive as a question about the verb
questions.stem: Explain to a learner how a Spanish speaker decides between an infinitive and a gerund after a verb such as empezar, volver or intentar, and say why both forms exist.

answer.exemplar: The decision is made by the first verb, not by the second, and that is the whole difficulty. A verb of beginning takes an infinitive with a, as in empezó a esperar, and a verb of repetition takes a gerund, as in siguió esperando, so the same waiting is presented once as a point of departure and once as a stretch of time. A verb of trying, intentar, takes an infinitive, and a verb of keeping on, continuar, takes a gerund, and neither can be swapped for the other without a change in what the sentence says about the speaker. The reason both forms exist is that Spanish has two ways of looking at an activity: the gerund presents it as a thing happening, with its own duration, and the infinitive presents it as a thing the first verb has something done with, which is why a second verb can also be attached, as in empezó a esperar el tren. A learner who tries to find a general rule about the second verb will be guessing, so the practical advice is to learn the pair with the first verb: whichever of the two the first verb normally takes is the one to reach for, and the exception is worth learning when it appears.

questions.explanation: A learner who is taught that either form is possible tends to treat the choice as a matter of style, and then writes sentences that are grammatical and misplace the emphasis. The reason the choice matters is that the two forms answer two different questions about the activity: is this a moment that has arrived, or is this a stretch that is going on? Learning the pair with the governing verb, rather than as two shapes to be chosen between, is what removes the guesswork, and it also explains why the same sentence can be heard twice in conversation with a slight difference of meaning that neither speaker would call a mistake. The two forms also behave differently in the negative and with a following clause, which is a further reason to treat them as different pieces of grammar rather than as alternatives.
questions.hint: Ask which verb makes the choice, and what each of the two forms makes the activity look like.

The test given in the two stages is short enough to be used while speaking, which is what makes it worth learning: ask who owns the thing being acted on. questions.explanation: The two features arrive together and they are the two features of voseo: the pronoun vos for the person addressed, and the second person forms built on the third person of the present, so podés where Spain would say puedes. Both are ordinary in the Río de la Plata and in a large part of Latin America, and both are absent from peninsular Spanish, where the same shopkeeper would say puedes. The second reading has the pronoun wrong, since usted is not a familiar form, the third confuses vos with vosotros and gets the number wrong, and the fourth mistakes a regional form for a feature of writing. What matters for a learner is that vos marks familiarity and not informality in general.
questions.hint: Ask which pronoun addresses the customer, and which ending the verb carries.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: say what a diminutive changes besides the size of a thing
questions.stem: A speaker says, 'Tenemos una casita en el campo.' What does the diminutive on casita add to the word besides size?

options.text: A sense of affection or of smallness that makes the house sound valued rather than merely small
A sense of doubt, so the speaker is no longer sure the house in the country really exists
options.misconception: reads a diminutive as a marker of doubt about a thing

options.text: A sense of distance, so the house is being mentioned as somebody else's rather than the speaker's
options.misconception: reads a diminutive as a sign that the noun belongs to somebody else

options.text: A sense of age, so the word is used for an old building rather than for a newly built one
options.misconception: believes a diminutive is a marker of age in a noun

questions.explanation: A diminutive does two jobs at once, and both are visible in casita: it makes the noun small, and it makes the speaker's attitude towards it warmer, since a thing described this way is a thing one is fond of. The suffix -ita is the one most often used with houses and with names of things one likes, and the same suffix on an adjective makes it milder rather than smaller. It does not cast doubt on the existence of the house, it does not move the house to somebody else's, and it says nothing about when the house was built. The check for a learner is to ask what the speaker would have said if the house were large and unloved, since a word for that is not la casa.
questions.hint: Ask what the word would be if the house were large and the speaker did not care for it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Order of the clauses in a long sentence
questions.learningObjective: order the parts of a sentence built on a condition, a purpose and a result
questions.stem: Four parts of one long sentence have been printed out of order. Which sequence makes a sentence a native speaker would accept?

options.text: Aunque seguía nevando, a clause of concession that sets an obstacle aside
los operarios de la carretera sacaron las máquinas, the main clause naming the action
para retirar la nieve de la calzada, an infinitive stating the purpose of the action
antes de que empezara el tráfico de la mañana, a time clause closing the sentence

questions.explanation: The order of a long sentence is not free, and the sequence below is the one a Spanish speaker produces. A clause of concession comes first because it is the condition the rest of the sentence is read against, and it is followed by the main clause, which is the part that carries the new information. The purpose infinitive then says what the action was for, and it is attached to the verb it explains rather than to the concession, so it cannot be moved in front of the main clause without changing the sentence. The time clause closes it, which is the usual position for one that fixes a deadline. A learner who puts the purpose first will produce a sentence that says what was intended before saying who did it, and one who puts the time clause first will have the morning traffic as the setting rather than the limit.
questions.hint: Ask which clause the rest of the sentence is read against, and which verb the infinitive explains.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: decide which clauses a Spanish speaker would put in the subjunctive
questions.stem: Five clauses are listed. Three of them are the kind a Spanish speaker puts in the subjunctive after si, aunque or a menos que. Which three?

options.text: aunque haga frío, saldremos a caminar
a menos que llueva, iremos en coche
si el tren llega temprano, llegaré a la reunión a las nueve
options.misconception: reads a condition the writer expects to hold as though it were a supposition

options.text: aunque había nevado, la carretera estaba limpia
options.misconception: believes aunque always takes the subjunctive whatever the fact is

options.text: si tuviera tiempo, escribiría una novela entera

questions.explanation: The three that take the subjunctive are the ones in which the writer does not assert the fact. Haga frío in an aunque clause is a cold that may or may not arrive, llueva in a menos que clause is rain that has not happened yet, and tuviera tiempo is a supply of time the writer does not count on. The other two stay in the indicative, and the reasons are different: si el tren llega is a condition the writer expects to hold, so it is a first-type conditional, and aunque había nevado concedes a snowfall that is treated as a fact. A learner who reads every si as unreal will turn the first of these into a daydream, and a learner who thinks aunque always takes the subjunctive will find that the fourth sentence is the ordinary way to say a thing that really happened.
questions.hint: Ask, of each clause, whether the writer asserts the fact or leaves it open.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: teach the difference between a clause that is doubtful and a clause that is merely unknown
questions.stem: Explain to a learner why Spanish sometimes keeps the indicative in a clause after si or cuando even though the fact is not known, and give the test that tells the two cases apart.

answer.exemplar: The subjunctive is not a machine for unknowns, and a learner who treats it as one will change verbs that should stay put. The distinction is between a fact the speaker asserts and a matter the speaker leaves open. In Se que el tren llega a las nueve the arrival is asserted, so the indicative is right even though a listener has not been told it. In No se si el tren llega a las nueve the arrival is exactly what is not known, so the indicative gives way to the subjunctive, and the same pair appears with the verb escribir. The practical test is to put the verb of knowing in front of the clause and ask whether the claim is one of knowledge, in which case the indicative survives, or one of ignorance, in which case the subjunctive is used. A second test is available for si, since a speaker who says si llueve is supposing a possibility while a speaker who says si llueve, no ira is conceding a fact that is not in dispute.

questions.explanation: Learners who have been taught that the subjunctive marks uncertainty usually get the right answer for negatives and the wrong one for positives, because a sentence such as creo que el tren llega contains a verb of opinion and a fact that is being asserted, and no amount of caution about the evidence should change its mood. The rule that fixes this is about the speaker's stance rather than about the listener's knowledge: a verb of knowing or asserting keeps the indicative, and a verb of not knowing, doubting or supposing takes the subjunctive. The second failure is a clause introduced by si where the speaker is not supposing anything at all but conceding a fact, as in si es cierto, no podemos hacer otra cosa, and the two are separated by the intent of the speaker rather than by the tense of anything.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker is asserting the clause or leaving it open.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A relative clause about a thing and about a whole clause
questions.learningObjective: tell a relative clause that points at a noun from one that points at a whole clause
questions.stem: Stage one: say what the word lo in 'Eso que me dijiste ayer' refers to. Stage two: say what que refers to in 'La casa que compraron tiene un jardín,' and state what tells the two apart.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: in eso que me dijiste ayer the lo is part of the pronoun eso and the whole phrase points at a thing or a matter the speaker has in mind, so the clause after que is about what was said, not about a noun that comes before it. Stage two: in La casa que compraron tiene un jardín the word que points back at la casa, and the clause tells a reader which house is meant, since a reader who did not know would otherwise be looking at two houses. What tells them apart is whether there is a noun for the clause to modify: a relative clause about a thing follows its noun, and a clause about a whole event is introduced by lo que, que or como and stands on its own. A learner who uses que for the first will produce a sentence whose que appears to modify eso, which is not something a Spanish speaker will do, and the result is a sentence about a thing rather than about what was said.

questions.explanation: The two stages fail in different ways, and the second is the one a learner tends to get right for the wrong reason, since a relative clause after a noun is the common case in every language. The case worth teaching is the one with no noun to modify, where Spanish reaches for lo que and the clause stands on its own, as in lo que me dijiste ayer, and the same construction turns up with como in eso que has dicho el jefe. A second distinction is worth adding at the two-stage level: a clause introduced by lo que says that the speaker is not naming a thing, whereas a clause introduced by que after a noun identifies one, and a learner who confuses them will produce a sentence that names nothing at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether there is a noun immediately before the que for the clause to modify.
